To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the renal medullary carbonyl stress, induced by high salt intake, is a key factor in the development of salt‐sensitive and obesity‐induced hypertension.
renal medullary reactive oxygen and carbonyl stress are important factors in the development of salt‐sensitive and obesity‐associated hypertension.

the development of salt‐sensitive (or salt‐induced) hypertension is associated with increased oxidative and carbonyl stress, which is caused by increased production of reactive oxygen and carbonyl species in the renal medulla and/or increased susceptibility of renal medullar cells to the damaging effects of these species.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of oxidative and/or carbolytic stress in salt‐induced hypertension in the rat.
the hypothesis that renal medullary oxidant and/or carbonyls stress plays a major role in the development and maintenance of hypertension and diabetes.
the hypothesis that the renal medulla is the primary site for the initiation and maintenance of salt‐sensitive (low renin) hypertension.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the renal medulla is a key target for salt‐sensitive hypertensive and diabetic patients.
renal medullary carbonyl and oxidative stresses are important in the development of salt‐sensitive and diabetes‐related hypertension.

renal medullary carbonyl stress, as a result of oxidative stress and/or increased carbonyl metabolism, is a common denominator of the pathophysiology of salt‐sensitive (or salt‐resistant) hypertension and diabetes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
oxidative and/or carbolytic stress in the renal medulla is an important factor in salt‐sensitivity.

the development of hypertension and diabetes is associated with a reduction in the activity of antioxidant enzymes, an increase in the activity of prooxidant enzymes and a decrease in the activity of carbonyl‐removing enzymes, which leads to an increase in the levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and reactive carbonyl species (RCS), and to an increase in oxidative and/or carbolytic stress.

the renal medulla is a major target for salt‐sensitive hypertensive and/or diabetic patients and the renal medullary carbonyl stress is a novel mechanism involved in the development and progression of this type of disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
oxidative stress, which is a major component of the pathophysiology of hypertension, is also a major component of renal injury.
oxidative stress and carbonyl stress are important in the development of salt‐sensitive (and salt‐resistant) hypertension.
renal medullary carbonyl stress is a major contributor to the development of salt‐sensitive (and salt‐induced) hypertension.
